query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Transitioning from conventional high‐thermal‐load, fusion‐based AM to a solid-state additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) process for AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will significantly reduce residual thermal stresses and preserve or enhance mechanical properties in miniature components.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock produced via mechanical alloying with near-spherical particle morphology optimized for flow and deposition.
generation.intervention: Employ a modified AFSD process adapted for miniature components, where a non-fusion, solid-state deposition is achieved by applying severe plastic deformation under controlled tool pressure and rotation.
generation.conditions: Processing window to be maintained at temperatures well below the melting point (targeting interfacial temperatures below ~0.4-0.5 Tm) with controlled deposition speeds on small-scale geometries (e.g., components with dimensions on the order of 5–10 mm), under ambient or protective inert atmosphere, and using a deposition tool with a fine tip to ensure feature resolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined equiaxed grain structure produced via severe plastic deformation during deposition, which minimizes thermal gradients and eliminates melting-related defects.
generation.mechanism: By preventing liquefaction and subsequent rapid solidification, the process avoids high localized thermal gradients responsible for residual stress buildup. The imposed plastic deformation refines the microstructure and relieves local stresses, ensuring improved mechanical properties relative to conventional fusion-based AM.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components fabricated via the modified AFSD process will exhibit a reduction in tensile residual stresses (anticipated reduction on the order of 30% or more compared to conventional laser AM) alongside improved yield strength and fatigue performance, with reduced processing complexity by eliminating post-process stress relief steps.
generation.baseline: Miniature components produced by conventional high-thermal-load, fusion-based additive manufacturing (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) that typically show high residual stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and require complex post-deposition processing.
generation.boundary: The intervention’s effectiveness is expected to be optimal for miniature components (dimensions up to approximately 1 cm^3) and may require further scaling adjustments for larger geometries or different alloy systems.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the adaptation of AFSD process parameters to the fine scale required for miniature components, potential variations in powder feedstock behavior under severe plastic deformation, and the reproducibility of the refined microstructures across complex geometries.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components: one set using the conventional high-thermal-load fusion-based AM process (e.g., LPBF) and the other using the modified AFSD process. Ensure both sets have identical geometries and similar dimensions. Use controlled deposition parameters with the AFSD set maintained in a solid-state regime. Post-fabrication, perform identical testing on both sets.
measurements: Residual stress distribution measured via X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction.
Mechanical properties characterized through tensile testing (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, fatigue testing).
Microstructural analysis via scanning electron microscopy and electron backscatter diffraction to assess grain size and phase distribution.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the AFSD-fabricated components do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., at least a 30% decrease) in tensile residual stresses and do not show equal or superior mechanical properties (yield strength and fatigue performance) compared to conventionally produced components, then the hypothesis is falsified.

For Al6063, the post-processing T6 heat treatment was reported to eliminate the hardness gradient similar to that noted in Figure 4a–c []. The solutionising step of the T6 heat treatment process exposes the material to a temperature greater than 500 °C [], which softens the material and allows for plastic flow and residual stress relief. Meanwhile, during the quenching and ageing steps, a different residual stress profile is expected to form, which is dependent on the structure geometry [].

Metal additive manufacturing (AM) is a low-cost, high-efficiency functional mold manufacturing technology. However, when the functional section of the mold or part is not a partial area, and large-area additive processing of high-hardness metal is required, cracks occur frequently in AM and substrate materials owing to thermal stress and the accumulation of residual stresses. Hence, research on residual stress reduction technologies is required. In this study, we investigated the effect of reducing residual stress due to thermal deviation reduction using a real-time heating device as well as changes in laser power in the AM process for both high-hardness cold and hot work mold steel. The residual stress was measured using an X-ray stress diffraction device before and after AM. Compared to the AM processing conditions at room temperature (25 °C), residual stress decreased by 57% when the thermal deviation was reduced. The microstructures and mechanical properties of AM specimens manufactured under room-temperature and real-time preheating and heating conditions were analyzed using an optical microscope. papers.system: Aluminium alloys processed via AFSD (a solid‐state additive manufacturing process)
papers.approach: Investigation of multiple-pass AFSD builds to study microstructure, residual stresses, and mechanical properties
papers.findings: AFSD produced deposits with very low residual stresses relative to fusion processes; however, deposit geometry and deposition path can still affect stress distribution and dimensional accuracy
papers.mechanism: Avoidance of melting and solidification‐induced thermal gradients by using a solid‐state process, leading to refined equiaxed grain structures with lower residual stress

papers.title: Residual Stress Reduction Technology in Heterogeneous Metal Additive Manufacturing.
papers.system: High-hardness mold steels processed by laser additive manufacturing
papers.approach: In situ thermal management through real-time preheating and adjustment of laser power during deposition
papers.findings: Using real-time heating to reduce thermal deviation resulted in a 57% decrease in residual stresses compared with room-temperature builds; benefits were confirmed on both small-scale and larger curved specimens
papers.mechanism: Reduction in thermal gradients during processing lowers the driving force for residual stress accumulation

papers.title: Modification of Residual Stresses in Laser Additive Manufactured AlSi10Mg Specimens Using an Ultrasonic Peening Technique.
papers.system: AlSi10Mg parts fabricated using Selective Laser Melting (SLM)
papers.approach: Application of ultrasonic peening to the as-built parts to modify the near-surface residual stress state
papers.findings: Post-process ultrasonic peening converted tensile stresses (up to 50 MPa) into compressive stresses (down to −150 MPa), improving mechanical performance and fatigue life
papers.mechanism: High-frequency mechanical peening introduces plastic deformation near the surface to re-balance the stress state from tensile to compressive

established: High thermal gradients inherent to fusion-based AM processes lead to significant residual stresses and degraded mechanical properties.
Solid-state processing approaches such as AFSD can effectively mitigate melting-induced defects including residual stresses and cracking.
In situ thermal management (preheating) and post-process interventions (ultrasonic peening, low-temperature heat treatments) have demonstrated significant reductions in residual stress.

approaches_tried.approach: Solid-state additive manufacturing (e.g., additive friction stir deposition)
approaches_tried.outcome: Marked reduction in residual stresses without the detrimental effects associated with melting; better microstructural refinement under the correct deposition parameters

approaches_tried.approach: Real-time process preheating during laser deposition
approaches_tried.outcome: Up to 57% decrease in residual stresses through reduced thermal gradients, though requiring additional system complexity

approaches_tried.approach: Ultrasonic peening as a post-process treatment
approaches_tried.outcome: Conversion of tensile to compressive residual stresses, potentially enhancing fatigue performance, but adds a separate process step
Relief of residual stresses with trade-offs in yield strength and possible grain coarsening

mechanisms: Avoidance of the liquefaction and rapid solidification stage reduces the formation of thermal gradients that cause residual stresses.
In situ preheating reduces the thermal deviation during deposition, lowering the stress buildup.
Mechanical surface treatments (e.g., ultrasonic peening) induce beneficial compressive stresses through plastic deformation.
Low-temperature annealing allows for stress relaxation via localized recrystallization without full melting.
disagreements: While heat treatments effectively relieve residual stress, some studies report deleterious effects on yield strength and microstructural integrity due to grain coarsening.

The balance between eliminating residual stress and preserving fine microstructures appears to be process- and material-dependent, with different approaches sometimes leading to trade-offs in mechanical performance.
open_questions: How will a solid-state process (such as an adapted form of additive friction stir deposition) perform specifically on AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock for miniature components?

What is the optimal processing window (temperature, deposition rate, and number of passes) for minimizing residual stresses while maintaining superior mechanical properties in this high-entropy alloy system?

Can a single intervention be engineered to simultaneously overcome residual thermal stresses, microstructural degradation, and processing complexity, without necessitating additional post-process steps?
opportunities: Investigate the direct adaptation of solid-state additive manufacturing methods (e.g., a modified AFSD process) to process AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock for miniature components.
Test a hybrid process intervention that combines in situ low-level preheating with a solid-state deposition regime, potentially eliminating the need for separate post-processing stress relief steps.

Explore optimized process parameters (e.g., deposition speed, layer thickness, and preheating temperature) tailored to the unique thermomechanical behavior of AlCrFeNiSi to achieve both low residual stress and superior mechanical properties.

Conduct a falsification experiment comparing components produced under conventional high-thermal-load conditions with those made by the proposed single-intervention process to quantify improvements in residual stress profile and mechanical performance.

directions.direction: Adopting a solid‐state deposition process (modified additive friction stir deposition) to avoid melting and rapid solidification.
directions.assessment: This approach directly addresses thermal gradients by eliminating melting; it builds on established evidence that AFSD reduces residual stresses (PMC11277587::web::002::abstract, PMC11277587::web::024::3_3_residual_stress_distribution) and refines microstructure. It fits the mini-component constraint but requires adaptation for small-scale features.

directions.direction: Implementing in situ substrate and powder preheating during deposition to reduce temperature gradients.
directions.assessment: In situ preheating lowers the thermal deviation, reducing residual stress (PMC7730888::web::000::abstract). However, it adds control complexity and may not fully eliminate degraded mechanical properties due to melt‐processing.

directions.direction: Utilizing a post‐process ultrasonic peening treatment to transform tensile into compressive stresses.
directions.assessment: Ultrasonic peening effectively modifies residual stress profiles (PMC6384986::web::000::abstract) and improves fatigue life, but as a post‐process step it does not simplify the processing regime and adds an additional manufacturing operation.

directions.direction: Applying a low‐temperature, in situ stress relief heat treatment immediately following deposition.
directions.assessment: Low-temperature annealing can relieve residual stresses (PMC12113129::web::003::abstract), yet it may inadvertently cause grain coarsening or compromise yield strength, and it still represents an extra process step.

directions.direction: Optimizing energy density during conventional laser‐based melting to control cooling rates and hence residual tensions.
directions.assessment: Adjustments to laser power and scan speed can reduce overall thermal gradients; however, the inherent high-thermal-load nature of fusion processing limits the achievable improvements in both residual stresses and mechanical properties.

choice.direction: Adopting a solid‐state deposition process (modified additive friction stir deposition)
choice.why: This direction directly overcomes the key limitations by eliminating the melting stage that produces steep thermal gradients. The evidence supporting the effectiveness of AFSD in reducing residual stresses, refining microstructure, and simplifying processing (as seen in aluminium systems, PMC11277587::web::002::abstract and PMC11277587::web::024::3_3_residual_stress_distribution) makes it a compelling single intervention. Its adaptation to AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, although challenging at miniature scales, promises both mechanical integrity and reduced residual thermal stresses without an additional post-process step.
